summary:
Review of a single-token staking pool with a Synthetix-style reward distributor, deployed on KUB Chain.

One Critical and one High issue were found in reward accounting, plus a centralization finding inherent to the KAP-20 reward token. Fixing C-01 requires a redeploy; the pool holds user principal and reward funds in the same balance.
trust_assumptions: `owner` is a 3/5 multisig; a single-EOA owner would raise M-01 to High.
The KAP-20 reward token's `Committee` address is out of scope and is trusted not to call `adminTransfer` against the pool.
Compiler `solc 0.8.24`, no unchecked blocks outside the audited ones.

sections.title: Method & verification
sections.body:
Reviewed across five dimensions: access control, reward-settlement logic, value accounting, low-level Solidity safety, and reward-curve mathematics.

Every candidate finding was re-checked with the goal of refuting it — accounting for checked arithmetic in solc 0.8.24, the clean OpenZeppelin ERC-20 with no transfer hooks, and the 2300-gas `.transfer` semantics on the payout path. **13 verified findings, 8 distinct after de-duplication**, reported most-severe first.

Produced with `model: opus`, `effort: high`, `solc 0.8.24`, Slither 0.10.x, at commit `a1b2c3d`.

sections.title: Reward solvency under load
sections.body: The pool's solvency invariant is `rewardToken.balanceOf(this) >= totalStaked + rewardRate * DURATION`. Because C-01 funds rewards from the shared balance, the invariant is already violated at deployment. Simulated over one reward period at the configured rate:

sections.title: Appendix A — parameters used
sections.body: Every quantitative claim above traces back to these values, read from the deployed contract at the audited commit.

roadmap.fixes:
Separate the reward reserve from staked principal and assert solvency on every top-up. Settle rewards before `emergencyWithdraw` zeroes the stake. Replace the unbounded `stakers[]` loop with the existing pull path.

While any of these is open the pool is not safe to operate with user funds.
roadmap.outcome: Principal is safe and always withdrawable

roadmap.fixes: `SafeCast` on every narrowing write plus `Math.mulDiv` for the intermediate. Express fees in basis points and read `decimals()` per token instead of hardcoding 1e18. Exclude both token addresses explicitly from `recoverERC20` rather than relying on them coinciding. Add a timelock to the owner multisig.
roadmap.outcome: No silent state corruption; key compromise is survivable

roadmap.fixes: Move reward accrual from `block.number` to `block.timestamp` with a per-second rate. Emit events on every privileged setter.
roadmap.outcome: Advertised APR holds across chains; changes are monitorable

findings.title: `notifyRewardAmount` counts staked principal as rewards
findings.description: The reward token and the staking token are the same address. `notifyRewardAmount` derives the distributable amount from `rewardToken.balanceOf(address(this))`, which includes every user's deposited principal, rather than from a separately tracked reward reserve.
findings.impact: All staked principal is scheduled for distribution as rewards. Early claimers withdraw other users' deposits; the last users to withdraw find the pool empty. Total loss of deposited funds, no attacker privilege required beyond calling `claim()` first.
findings.recommendation: Track the reward reserve explicitly: `uint256 public rewardReserve;` incremented in a `depositRewards(uint256)` function that pulls tokens via `safeTransferFrom`, and compute `reward = rewardReserve` in `notifyRewardAmount`. Additionally assert solvency: `require(rewardToken.balanceOf(address(this)) >= totalStaked + rewardRate * DURATION)`.

findings.title: Rewards are not settled before `emergencyWithdraw` zeroes the stake
findings.description: `emergencyWithdraw` sets `user.amount = 0` and returns the principal without calling `_updateReward(msg.sender)` and without zeroing `user.rewardDebt`.
findings.impact: The stale `rewardDebt` remains claimable. A user calls `emergencyWithdraw`, re-deposits 1 wei, and then `claim()` pays out rewards accrued against the withdrawn principal. Theft is bounded by the reward reserve, so yield only, not principal.
findings.recommendation: Call `_updateReward(msg.sender)` at the top of `emergencyWithdraw` and zero `user.rewardDebt` alongside `user.amount`. Add an invariant test that `sum(pendingRewards) <= rewardReserve` after an interleaved deposit / emergencyWithdraw / claim sequence.

findings.title: Owner can withdraw the staking token via `recoverERC20`
findings.description:
`recoverERC20` excludes the reward token but not the staking token.

Because both are the same address here, the exclusion happens to cover it today — but the check is written against `rewardToken`, so any future redeploy with distinct tokens loses the protection.
findings.impact: Under the current configuration the drain path is closed. In a redeploy with separate tokens, the owner multisig could withdraw all staked principal. Rated Medium because the owner is a 3/5 multisig and the current wiring is safe.
findings.recommendation: Exclude both addresses explicitly: `require(token != address(stakeToken) && token != address(rewardToken), "protected");` — do not rely on them coinciding.

findings.title: Unbounded loop over `stakers[]` bricks `distribute()` permanently
findings.description:
`distribute()` iterates the `stakers` array, which any address can grow by staking 1 wei. Each iteration performs a storage write (~5,000 gas), so the call exceeds the block gas limit at roughly 6,000 entries.

KUB Chain gas is cheap, so an attacker can add those entries for a few dollars — this is an economically realistic attack here, not a theoretical one.
findings.impact: Once the array passes the gas-limit threshold, `distribute()` reverts on every call and can never succeed again — rewards are permanently undistributable. The array cannot shrink, so there is no recovery without an upgrade. Attacker cost is a few dollars in gas; damage is the full reward reserve.
findings.recommendation: Replace push distribution with the pull pattern already present in `_updateReward` — users claim their own rewards in O(1) and no loop over stakers is needed. If a loop must stay, paginate it (`distribute(uint256 start, uint256 end)`), cache `stakers.length` outside the loop, and use `unchecked { ++i; }`.

findings.title: `uint128` cast in `UserInfo` truncates silently for high-supply tokens
findings.description:
`UserInfo.rewardDebt` is packed as `uint128` and written with an unchecked cast. `rewardDebt = amount * accRewardPerShare / 1e12` exceeds `type(uint128).max` (~3.4e38) once `amount * accRewardPerShare` grows past that bound, which is reachable for an 18-decimal token with a large supply over a long accrual period.

Downcasts are **not** checked by Solidity 0.8 — the value wraps silently rather than reverting.
findings.impact: A wrapped `rewardDebt` makes `pending = accrued - rewardDebt` underflow and revert, freezing that user's claim and withdrawal path, or — if it wraps the other way — pays out rewards that were never funded. Rated Medium because it requires a large supply and long accrual; High for a token above ~1e30 total supply.
findings.recommendation: Use `SafeCast.toUint128` on every narrowing write so truncation reverts instead of corrupting state, and use `Math.mulDiv` for the intermediate so `amount * accRewardPerShare` cannot overflow before the division. Widening `rewardDebt` to `uint256` is the simpler fix and costs one extra storage slot.

findings.title: Fee math hardcodes 18 decimals — wrong for any 6- or 8-decimal fee token
findings.description:
`setFeeToken(address)` lets the owner change which token performance fees are collected in, but the fee calculation scales by a hardcoded `1e18` and the minimum-fee constant is expressed in absolute token units.

`decimals()` is not part of the mandatory ERC-20 standard and is not always 18: USDC and USDT are 6, WBTC is 8. The moment the fee token is set to any of them the maths is off by a factor of 1e12 or 1e10 — silently, with no revert.
findings.impact: With a 6-decimal fee token the computed fee is 1e12x too small, so the treasury collects effectively nothing and `MIN_FEE` can never be satisfied — every fee-collecting call reverts, blocking the path that depends on it. With a token of more than 18 decimals the scale-up overflows. No funds are stolen, but fees are either uncollectable or the path is bricked, and nothing signals it. Rated Medium because it requires the owner to use the setter; it becomes High the first time they do.
findings.recommendation: Express the fee in basis points of the amount rather than in a scaled absolute unit — that removes the decimals dependency entirely. Read `decimals()` from the token in `setFeeToken` and store it beside the address so it can never go stale, reject anything above 18, keep the minimum-fee threshold per token, and emit the decimals in the event so integrators can detect the change. Use `Math.mulDiv` so the intermediate cannot overflow before the division.

findings.title: Reward accrual uses `block.number`
findings.description: `_updateReward` accrues over `block.number - lastRewardBlock` with `rewardPerBlock` calibrated for ~5s KUB blocks.
findings.impact: Block time is not constant. The realized APR drifts from the advertised one whenever block production varies, and the same constant is wrong if the contract is ever deployed to another chain. No loss of funds.
findings.recommendation: Switch to `block.timestamp` and a `rewardPerSecond` rate. See `references/methodology.md` chain notes.

findings.title: Missing events on privileged setters
findings.description: `setRewardRate` and `setTreasury` change protocol-critical state without emitting an event.
findings.impact: No security impact. Off-chain monitoring and incident response cannot detect the change without polling storage.
findings.recommendation: Emit `RewardRateUpdated(uint256 oldRate, uint256 newRate)` and `TreasuryUpdated(address old, address new)`.
